verses.text: Yahweh  called to Moses, and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting, saying,
“Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘When anyone of you offers an offering to Yahweh, you shall offer your offering of the livestock, from the herd and from the flock.
“‘If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without defect. He shall offer it at the door of the Tent of Meeting, that he may be accepted before Yahweh.
He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.
He shall kill the bull before Yahweh. Aaron’s sons, the priests, shall present the blood and sprinkle the blood around on the altar that is at the door of the Tent of Meeting.
He shall flay the burnt offering, and cut it into pieces.
The sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire on the altar, and lay wood in order on the fire;
and Aaron’s sons, the priests, shall lay the pieces, the head, and the fat in order on the wood that is on the fire which is on the altar;
but its innards and its legs he shall wash with water. The priest shall burn all of it on the altar, for a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.
“‘If his offering is from the flock, from the sheep, or from the goats, for a burnt offering, he shall offer a male without defect.
He shall kill it on the north side of the altar before Yahweh. Aaron’s sons, the priests, shall sprinkle its blood around on the altar.
He shall cut it into its pieces, with its head and its fat. The priest shall lay them in order on the wood that is on the fire which is on the altar,
but the innards and the legs he shall wash with water. The priest shall offer the whole, and burn it on the altar. It is a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.
“‘If his offering to Yahweh is a burnt offering of birds, then he shall offer his offering of turtledoves or of young pigeons.
The priest shall bring it to the altar, and wring off its head, and burn it on the altar; and its blood shall be drained out on the side of the altar;
and he shall take away its crop with its filth, and cast it beside the altar on the east part, in the place of the ashes.

He shall tear it by its wings, but shall not divide it apart. The priest shall burn it on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.

footnotes.content: Yahweh speaks to Moses from the Tent of Meeting—the place where heaven and earth meet. Notice how the Lord doesn't shout from a distance; He draws near, intimate, inviting His people into the pattern of approach He Himself has set.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here the Tent of Meeting becomes school. The people learn that worship isn't accident or whim—it's a gift offered with intention. From your own herd, from what you own, you give. Genuine praise costs something.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A male without defect, brought to the door. You see here what the prophets will later denounce as mere ritual—yet here it's the only way Israel knows to say, 'I come as myself, with care, before the Lord's face.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The laying on of hands—that simple, profound gesture. The worshiper places themselves on the offering, saying without words: this is me, my life, my need to be made right before You. Intercession begins here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the door of the Tent—in plain sight, not hidden—the blood is shed before Yahweh. Blood poured out speaks what words cannot: the cost of approach, the gravity of atonement. Later, a greater blood will speak the same language, once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The animal is flayed and cut into pieces. There's no sentimentality here—the text is unflinching. Real devotion means surrendering the whole of yourself, not just the pleasant parts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fire on the altar, wood laid in order. You can almost see the priest's hands, arranging each piece with care. The Lord is met not by chaos but by order, by hands that know their work and do it faithfully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Piece by piece, the offering rises in order on the wood—head, fat, each part in its place. There's something holy in this careful arrangement, as if even in dismantling the animal, the priest honors it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The innards and legs washed with water—cleanliness itself becomes part of the offering. And the smoke rises as 'a pleasant aroma to Yahweh.' The Lord doesn't want cruelty; He wants the whole person, washed clean and offered up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you own sheep or goats instead of cattle, you can still come. The path to approach God isn't limited by wealth. A poor person with a goat stands equal before the Lord's face with a rich person and an ox.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The north side of the altar—a specific place, not a vague direction. Even geography matters in approach. The Lord knows where we stand and calls us to remember: worship is concrete, particular, real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cut into pieces, head and fat laid in order on the fire. The rhythm repeats—not to bore us, but to show us that the way of approach is steady, sure, not made up as we go. The Lord's pattern never changes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again: innards washed, the whole burned, and it rises as 'a pleasant aroma.' The Lord doesn't overlook the hidden parts; He sees and accepts all of you, inside and out, when you come with an honest heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now even the poorest have a way forward: turtledoves or young pigeons. The gospel of access is already here—the widow, the stranger, the child with one small bird can meet God exactly as the wealthy do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest wrings off the head and burns it on the altar. Even a bird—small, common—is treated with the same reverence as an ox. Nothing offered to the Lord is too humble to honor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The crop with its filth is removed and cast aside—east, where the ashes collect. Even waste finds its place in the pattern. Nothing is wasted in the Lord's scheme; everything belongs somewhere.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Torn by its wings but not divided apart—the wholeness preserved even in tearing. Readers today hear an echo: Christ's body broken yet whole, offered up as 'a pleasant aroma,' the sacrifice that needs never to be repeated. All this law pointed here, as of 2026-10.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
